THE GLASS BALLOT BoxEs.-For some days
there has been good deal said about the glass
ballot boxes used at the late election in accord
ance with clause in the Metropolitan Police
bill of April last. How the contract was given
out and who was the real contractor have
been subjects of much discussion; and docu-
ment has been published for political purposes
pending the coming charter election, setting
forth one side Of the question, and alleging that
the contract for the manufacture Of these
boxes was fraudulently made-that the price
charged was more than three times the actual
cost-that the number ordered was considera-
bly, more than Is required; and furthermore
which is the gist of the whole afiair-that Fer
nando Wood is interested pecuniarily in the
transaction, through the medium of his brother
Benjamin. This document il part of the pro-
ceedings in a suit in the Supreme Court asking
for an injunction restraining the Mayor and
other officials from paying for the glass ballot
boxes. We publish to-day all the papers in the
case, showing both sides of the question, and
putting the boot on the right leg. They are
very interesting, as indications of the shifts to
which politicians will resort in time Of need.

GRAsH0PPERS IN MINNEsToA.-A letter from
Anoka, Minnesota Territory, fully confirms
the one lately published about the destruction
of crops by the grasshopper army travelling
south from Red River. The writer says


Their favorite food is tender garden vege-
tables, beans. onions, carrots, turnips, &c. Po-
tatOes are ruined by being Invested Of all
leaves. Last season they arrived too late to
destroy wheat and corn. But considering their
immense numbers, the ground being literal y
covered with them in many places farmers con-
sidered themselves lucky in getting rid of them
as easily as they did. for with the sharp frosts
OF autumn and the disappearance of vegetation
they gradually died off. But this was not the
end thereof 1t seems that eating did not oc-
cupy all their time or attention. Careful OBJ
servers saw them busy upon the ground about
something, which now proves to have been de-
posting their eggs, which, naturalists say, the
females lay to the number of one hundred and
fifty. We had very severe weather here last
winter, the mercury several times sinking more
than forty degrees below zero, yet those eggs,
almost on the surface of the ground as they
were, came cut brighten the spring As soon
as the snow was gone, and the ground began to
get warm, the grashoppers began to come up,
sOme early and others later, according to the
situation the eggs had to the sun. They have
been Matching ever since, and presume are
not all out yet. ... -


When first hatched they are quite light in
color, and but small in size. But there are two
things that they can do fright smart from the
first, viz: hop and eat. They hop first, and keep
hopping till they find something that suits them
to eat and they are nowise dainty about it either,
for they don't stop till the supply is exhausted
OF course the consequences are most disastrous
Whole acres of wheat are completely eaten and
destroyed in a day. Oats fare no better, and
corn will doubtless share the same fate Some
farmers, becoming discouraged, stopped short
in their planting and sowing declaring they
would not waste their seed. Others put in their
whole crop, but with faint prospect of getting
back anything Some have hoped that they
would leave, which they doubtless will do when
they get wings, which will not be, fear, till
everything in the way of crops is destroyed As
yet they don't eat grass much, but of course
when other things are gone they will take that
and then stock must suffer. Water treatment
seems to suit them, for they are all the smarter
after a hard rain. They come from the West
and travel East; and when they have eaten
everything in Minnesota, Iowa, Wisconsin and
Illinois will have to share the same fate, as our
stock is sufficient for all the country below US

We dlned last week with a French Countess
Your American Imagination may, perhaps,
fancy lavish display and abundant waste but
no-the house was small, though arranged and
furnished with the most elegant taste. The
lady would not have been a true French woman
had she expended money in useless superfiui-
tics. The dinner, which was quite perfect in n
certain way, might be characterized in a like
manner. There was not too much of anything
and yet plenty. Abundance did not appear
90 much as tasteful and beautiful arrangement.
Surprisingly delicate, too, were the sauces.
For instance, after many dishes, there was
served a roast turkey, which 1 supposed was
like all other roast turkeys-very good but
was surprised upon adding the sauce to a good
nutritious bit of the breast. / discovered q
new and unexpected fayor-something that
did not remember to have tasted at an Ameri-
can table.


names of the courses, thinking that it NAV help

silver epergne as you might have seen on some
more extravagant table-but large pyramid
of beautiful camelias, roses and viOlets, buried
IN their fresh-lOOking green moss, with here and
there peeping out a little pot of ripe strawber-
ries-tOr 1t was February, and they were then
rarity-the whole rising from low, brown
wicker basket. The china-that is; the plates
for no dishes were placed on the table, as the
walters, who numbered only two, handed every
dish, it being first well carved on a side table

all. After small rich oyster pates was served

panied by simple potatoes. Then lamb chops

parsley cut up fine. With each different course

chestnuts, which are favorte French bon bon
Finally, black coffee, served in cups and sau-

after the liqueurS and sweet cOrdals, we all

went 20 the drawing room. | thought, as we
came home, never fanced a dinner could be
so complete; yet with nothing very expensive,
nothing snowy or elaborate; yet every dish was
finished, and the whole artistically perfect.
